title: General Principles of Neurologic Localization
subtitle: How to localize from signs: where pathways cross, upper versus lower motor neuron patterns, sensory pathway levels, and what gait disorders point to

coreAnatomy.title: Corticospinal tract and the motor neuron

points.text: Ventral horn and brainstem motor neurons are the last link to muscle, the final common pathway.
points.quote: The motor neurons of the ventral horn of the spinal cord and the motor nuclei in the brainstem, whose axons synapse directly on striated muscles

points.text: The corticospinal tract runs through the corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, middle part of the peduncle and basis pontis.
points.quote: descend in the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle three-fifths of the cerebral peduncle, the basis pontis

points.text: Most fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation, so a lesion above it gives contralateral signs and one below it gives ipsilateral signs.
points.quote: approximately 90% of the corticospinal fibers in the pyramid cross the ventral midline

points.text: The pyramidal tract lies ventrally in the pons, which explains pure motor hemiparesis from pontine lesions.
points.quote: the ventral location of the pyramidal tract in the pons, a pure motor hemiparesis of brainstem origin is usually observed with pontine lesions

points.text: In the caudal posterior limb the arm fibers lie anterior to the trunk and leg fibers.
points.quote: fibers to the upper extremity are located more anteriorly (i.e., shoulder, elbow, wrist, fingers), followed by fibers to the trunk

points.text: Corticobulbar fibers pass through the genu, which accounts for the face and tongue weakness with little limb involvement of the capsular genu syndrome.
points.quote: Corticobulbar fibers, and perhaps motor corticopontine fibers, occupy the genu of the internal capsule.

points.text: The anterior limb is supplied by the recurrent artery of Heubner; the genu and the lower posterior limb by the anterior choroidal artery; the upper portions by lenticulostriate branches.
points.quote: The anterior limb of the internal capsule receives its vascular supply from the recurrent artery of Heubner, a branch of the anterior cerebral artery

points.text: The lower face has predominantly crossed corticobulbar input, while the upper face is represented in both hemispheres.
points.quote: the muscles of the lower face receive predominantly crossed corticobulbar input

points.text: Pain and temperature fibers cross in the anterior commissure and ascend contralaterally as the spinothalamic tracts.
points.quote: Axons from secondary sensory neurons in the dorsal horn decussate at the anterior spinal cord commissure, ascending in the contralateral anterolateral funiculi

points.text: In the cervical spinothalamic tract, sacral fibers are most superficial, so deep intrinsic cord lesions can spare sacral sensation.
points.quote: at cervical levels, fibers from sacral segments are found most superficially

points.text: Fasciculus gracilis carries sacral, lumbar and lower thoracic roots; the upper thoracic and cervical roots form the lateral fasciculus cuneatus.
points.quote: Sacral, lumbar, and approximately the lower six thoracic roots contribute to the medially located fasciculus gracilis

points.text: Dorsal column nuclei fibers cross in the lower medulla to form the medial lemniscus.
points.quote: Axons from neurons in both nuclei cross the midline at the lower medulla and form the medial lemniscus.

points.text: In the postcentral gyrus the calf and foot are medial and the face is lateral.
points.quote: the calf and foot represented medially, followed by the thigh, abdomen, thorax, shoulder, arm, forearm, hand, digits, and face

points.text: Standing and walking need sensory input (proprioception, vision, vestibular) and motor output.
points.quote: the act of standing and walking requires sensory information reaching specific brain centers and a motor output from these centers

points.text: Brainstem centers include the vestibular nuclei, reticular formation and the pedunculopontine and cuneiform nuclei.
points.quote: the vestibular nuclei, the medullary and pontine reticular formation, and the pedunculopontine and cuneiform nuclei at the junction between the pons and midbrain

points.text: Automatic gait depends on the cortico-putamino-pallido-thalamo-cortical loop.
points.quote: Critical for the performance of the automatic movements that constitute gait is the cortico-putamino-pallido-thalamo-cortical loop.

localizationRules.rule: The lesion is where two affected pathways cross
localizationRules.explanation: One sign alone fits many sites; combining two pathways narrows it down. A third nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis puts the lesion in the ipsilateral crus cerebri (Weber).
localizationRules.quote: the lesion is where the two affected pathways cross

localizationRules.explanation: Localize from the examination (including reported sensory findings); use the time course to guess the cause: minutes suggests vascular or epilepsy, days infection or demyelination, months tumor or degeneration.
localizationRules.quote: For the anatomic localization of lesions, the neurologic examination is much more important than the history.

localizationRules.rule: Side of signs relative to the pyramidal decussation
localizationRules.explanation: Upper motor neuron signs from a lesion above the decussation appear on the opposite side; from a lesion below it they appear on the same side.
localizationRules.quote: With lesions above the pyramidal decussation, the previously discussed signs are detected on the opposite side of the body

localizationRules.explanation: Upper motor neuron facial paresis on the same side as the hemiplegia points above the upper pons (motor cortex, corona radiata, internal capsule), though peduncle and upper pons lesions can also do this.
localizationRules.quote: the lesion is generally localizable above the upper pons; likely sites are the MC, corona radiata, or internal capsule

localizationRules.rule: Medial versus lateral medullary sensory loss
localizationRules.explanation: Medial medullary lesions affect the lemniscal modalities (vibration, position) and may spare the spinothalamic tract; lateral medullary lesions take pain and temperature instead.
localizationRules.quote: Impairment of vibratory and position sense on opposite side of the body, may spare the spinothalamic tract

keySyndromes.name: Weber syndrome (cerebral peduncle)
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral oculomotor paresis with pupillary involvement + contralateral hemiparesis including the lower face
keySyndromes.clue: Pyramidal fibers and the CN III fascicle are both damaged in the peduncle, so the third nerve palsy is on the side of the lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: causing an ipsilateral oculomotor paresis with pupillary involvement and a contralateral hemiparesis including the lower portion of the face

keySyndromes.name: Brown-Sequard (hemicord) syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron paralysis at the lesion level + ipsilateral spastic paralysis below it + ipsilateral loss of proprioception below it + contralateral loss of pain and temperature
keySyndromes.clue: Motor and posterior column signs are ipsilateral; the crossed spinothalamic tract causes contralateral pain and temperature loss.
keySyndromes.quote: ipsilateral spastic paralysis below the level of the lesion due to interruption of the descending corticospinal tract

keySyndromes.name: Lateral medullary sensory syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Loss of pain and temperature on the contralateral body (may spare medial lemniscus functions) + decreased pain and temperature on the ipsilateral face from the spinal tract and nucleus of CN V
keySyndromes.clue: The ipsilateral face with contralateral body pattern is hemianesthesia alternans.
keySyndromes.quote: decreased pain and temperature on the ipsilateral face and contralateral body (hemianesthesia alternans)

keySyndromes.name: Anterior choroidal artery territory infarction
keySyndromes.triad: Hemiparesis (corticospinal tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule) + hemisensory loss (thalamic radiations in the posterior limb) + hemianopia (optic tract, lateral geniculate body or optic radiations)
keySyndromes.clue: The combination of hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia suggests this territory.
keySyndromes.quote: hemisensory loss due to involvement of the superior thalamic radiations situated in the thalamogeniculate segment of the posterior limb of the internal capsule

keySyndromes.name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (spastic gait)
keySyndromes.triad: Severe: paraparesis + hand clumsiness with atrophy of small hand muscles; milder: unsteadiness with positive Romberg + inverted radial reflex + possible cervical sensory level to vibration
keySyndromes.clue: Usually at the C5-C6 interspace, with lesions in the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts; often progressive if untreated.
keySyndromes.quote: Severe lesions in this location result in paraparesis and clumsiness of the hand with atrophy in the small muscles of the hand.

keySyndromes.name: Magnetic gait (frontal gait disorder)
keySyndromes.triad: Cannot lift feet to walk although able to stand + feet seem glued to the floor, difficulty initiating gait and turning + preserved volitional leg movements (drawing figures with the feet, heel-shin)
keySyndromes.clue: Attributed to bilateral medial frontal cortex dysfunction with relative sparing of paracentral cortex; also severe hydrocephalus or bilateral ischemic white matter lesions. Arm swing may be preserved, unlike Parkinson disease.
keySyndromes.quote: these patients have such an inability to lift their feet and walk that their feet may seem to be glued to the floor

boardTraps.text: A hemiparesis that is disproportionate points to a laterally placed corticosubcortical lesion (faciobrachial) or to the paracentral region (crural); internal capsule lesions are usually proportionate, but capsular lesions may rarely give a faciobrachial or crural pattern.
boardTraps.quote: If the hemiparesis is disproportionate (e.g., faciobrachial predominance), the lesion is often corticosubcortical and laterally placed on the contralateral hemisphere.

boardTraps.text: A lesion confined to the cerebral peduncle or medullary pyramid can give weakness and hyperreflexia without spasticity.
boardTraps.quote: lesions confined to the medullary pyramid may cause weakness and hyperreflexia without spasticity

boardTraps.text: In cervical myelopathy the brachioradialis tap may give a brisk finger flexor response instead (inverted radial reflex).
boardTraps.quote: The brachioradialis reflex may be depressed, and instead, a brisk finger flexor response is elicited when percussing the brachioradialis tendon

boardTraps.text: Cerebellar lesions usually make the patient fall to the side of the lesion, but tonsillar-area lesions can reverse this.
boardTraps.quote: some patients with lesions in the tonsillar area develop increased tone (and increased reflexes) in the ipsilateral side and fall to the contralateral side

boardTraps.text: The cautious gait is common in older people but carries no localizing value.
boardTraps.quote: It may represent a milder or compensatory phase of any of the disorders mentioned above and it is not localizing.

boardTraps.text: Drop attacks in older people are more often due to central disequilibrium (subcortical hemispheric disease) than to vertebrobasilar disease.
boardTraps.quote: Central disequilibrium is probably the most common cause of the so-called drop attacks
